cells.tense: What has ended for you is being let end, and the next thing is already being trusted.
cells.act: let an exchange flow both ways
cells.ask: With someone you trade with — favors, rides, dinners — let the next one run its whole length untracked. Give without noting the balance, or take without squaring it afterward.
cells.core:
Some things have ended under your hands, and you're letting them stay ended. You can feel when something is finished, and you don't take it back for comfort or reopen it for a second pass. The clearing happens at a pace that isn't yours to hurry, and you trust it.

What comes next you let arrive rather than hauling it forward. That's rarer than it sounds. People see a door close and read it as a loss that has to be repaid. In your accounts it just closes.

So let one exchange run full length with someone you trade with — give without marking it, or take without squaring it afterward. One person, one exchange, nothing added. If the share lands uneven, sit with it rather than adjusting it the same day. You don't need the ledger here.
cells.sheetLine: What's finished, you let stay finished — even when no one says so.
cells.verb: ending what has finished so the new thing can start
cells.place: at the table where the shares are weighed and set right

cells.tense: Something is ending in your hands before it has had any life to spend.
cells.act: let yourself be reached by what they are carrying
cells.ask: At a moment this week when someone near you is carrying something heavy, let it land on you before you answer. Don't resolve it, don't fix it, don't leave the room.
cells.core:
Something is ending in your hands before it has lived. This project, this arrangement, this version of yourself — you're past each one before it has begun, and the rush feels like bravery. It isn't. The clearing that used to follow your sense of what's finished has become a standing policy, and things are being cut while they're green.

Deeper down something is being shed already; there's just no room to tell what should go next. What waits to be reached is what you've been moving too fast to touch.

At one heavy moment, let someone's load land on you before you answer — don't clear it, don't leave. And before you close the next thing, keep it running a week beyond where you'd have stopped it. See what it looks like still alive.

cells.tense: A door closed some time back, and you have not moved from the spot where it stood.
cells.act: go where the feeling is already pulling
cells.ask: Give an afternoon to whatever already has a pull on you — a person, a room, a piece of work — and follow it without deciding anything about the rest.
cells.core:
A door closed some time back and you're at the spot where it stood. You've been calling that loyalty. It might be — but nothing waits on the other side of it, and the days keep going by. What used to feel like holding on has turned into a way of not moving at all.

The share is out of true: you keep giving to something that's already over, and taking nothing back.

There's a pull in you somewhere. Follow it for an afternoon — a person, a room, a piece of work — and give it your whole attention. Notice where your energy actually wants to go. Nothing has to be settled about the old thing today; one afternoon, one direction, that's all.

cells.tense: Something is ending in you and the ending has not been given a name.
cells.act: give the mess a shape it can be carried in
cells.ask: Make a container for one confusing area of your life — a folder, a labeled box, a dated page. You don't have to fix what's in it, just make it hold.
cells.core:
Something is on its way out in you and it hasn't been written down. Not because you're hiding it — you just haven't looked directly, and the not-looking carries its own momentum. From the inside it feels like nothing is happening. From where others stand, you've been moving on for a while.

When this season does get named, it goes easier. The container comes first; the feelings catch up.

So make one for a messy area of your life — a folder, a labeled box, a dated page on the calendar. You don't have to fix the thing or understand it. You only have to make it possible to hold. What's ending will still be ending after, and the container is what carries it.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person is mid-ritual — that their endings or overhauls have a pattern underpinning them. A reader could fairly say 'no, the upheaval is real, nothing is holding it.' If wrong, the asks still stand, since each is a discrete small act (a letter, a drive, a container) and none depends on the reading being right. Serves me more than them: 'You keep ending what you only meant to change' — vivid, but it tells their story for them.
